result:
I wake up to the sound of the refrigerator humming through the wall and the light that comes in sideways across the ceiling. It is not morning yet in the way the calendar says it is, it's the kind of morning that feels like an afterthought. I lie there for a minute and count the things I can hear before I decide to get up: the fridge, a car somewhere far away, the faint tick of the heater, my own breathing. I like that pause because it is the only part of the day that is not assigned to anything.

Coffee is the first negotiation. I put the kettle on and watch the water. There's something about waiting for it to boil that makes me feel competent. While it heats I open the curtains. The street is wet. Someone has been watering plants or it rained in the night. The air smells like concrete and cut grass. I think about how many small decisions led to this exact moment: someone decided to build this building, someone decided to plant those trees, someone decided to leave a window open last night and let the cool air in. I am the sum of all those other people's decisions and my own inability to stay still.

I sit at the kitchen table with my notebook open to a blank page. The page is a kind of threat. I like the way the pen feels in my hand before I write, the weight of it, the way it balances. I used to fill notebooks with lists. Now I fill them with sentences I later cross out. The first line is always bad. The first line is always trying too hard to sound like the beginning of something important. I write it anyway and then I write under it: *This is not the beginning.* That helps.

The world is full of things that are happening without permission. A pigeon lands on the fire escape and pecks at nothing. A bus sighs at the stop. Somewhere a child is learning how to tie their shoes for the third time this week. I think about the idea of attention as a kind of love. We pay attention to what we think matters and then later we are surprised when it turns out we missed the thing that actually did. I am trying to practice a softer attention, one that notices the refrigerator hum and the way the steam curls off the mug and the way my neighbor practices violin at 7:15 every day, the same three measures over and over until it is finally clean.

I have a friend who says writing is just remembering out loud. I think it's more like trying to find the shape of a feeling in the dark with your hands. You bump into something hard and you say, "That is a word." You bump into something soft and you say, "That is a word too." Sometimes you find a phrase that fits perfectly and you hold onto it like a small animal. You don't know what it means yet, but you know it matters. I have a collection of those phrases in the notes on my phone. *The light was thin as paper.* *She laughed like she was apologizing.* *We were both tired of being brave.*

Today I want to write about the way time stretches when you are doing something with your hands. Washing dishes, folding laundry, kneading dough. The mind quiets down and then it starts to wander and then it starts to tell the truth. I was washing a mug this morning and I remembered being eight years old and watching my grandfather sand a piece of wood until it was smooth. He didn't talk. He just sanded. The smell of the wood filled the garage. I asked him what he was making and he said, "Something useful." He never told me what it was for. Years later I found it in the shed: a simple wooden box with a lid that fit perfectly. I still don't know what it was for.

The internet says we live in an age of distraction. Maybe we do. But distraction is just attention that hasn't found a home yet. I scroll, I read, I watch a video of someone restoring an old chair and I feel a strange kinship. There is comfort in watching someone else work slowly. I want to be the kind of person who can sand a piece of wood for an hour without checking my phone. I am not that person yet.

I think about the people I love and the way I try to remember them in detail. The way my sister tucks her hair behind her ear when she's thinking. The way my dad always puts his keys in the same bowl even though he loses them anyway. The way my mother hums when she cooks. These details feel like proof. If I can remember them, they are real. If I forget them, I am afraid they will disappear.

There is a line I keep coming back to: *We are all just trying to be less alone with our thoughts.* It is simple and it is true. Sometimes the best thing you can do for someone is to sit with them while they are quiet. Not to fix anything. Not to ask questions. Just to be there while the refrigerator hums.

I drink the coffee now. It is lukewarm. I was too busy watching the steam to drink it while it was hot. That is a metaphor for something but I won't make it one. Sometimes lukewarm is fine. Sometimes you learn to like the taste of coffee after it cools because it is less sharp and you can actually taste the bitterness and the sweetness at the same time.

The day is starting. Emails will come. The to-do list will grow. I will try to do the things I said I would do. I will probably forget something. I will probably make a mistake that I will have to apologize for later. I will probably also do something kind without thinking about it. A small thing. Holding the door. Sending a text that says *thinking of you.* Listening all the way through.

If you are reading this, you are also in the middle of your own morning. Maybe you are drinking tea. Maybe you haven't slept. Maybe you are writing your own 1000 words and wondering if anyone will read them. I hope you keep going. Write the bad first line. Write under it. Keep your collection of phrases. Pay attention to the refrigerator hum.

I am going to close the notebook now. The page is full. It is not perfect. It is not important. It is just what came to me. And that is enough for today.
